subproblem.title: A smooth mollifier sequence whose mollifications converge a.e. for every locally integrable function
subproblem.statement: Let n ∈ ℕ. There are functions ψ_k : ℝⁿ → ℝ (k ∈ ℕ) such that for every k: ψ_k is C^∞; ψ_k has compact support; spt ψ_k ⊆ B̄_{1/(k+1)}(0), where spt is the closed support (Lean: tsupport); ψ_k ≥ 0; and ∫ ψ_k dLⁿ = 1. Moreover, for every locally Lⁿ-integrable g : ℝⁿ → ℝ, (g ∗ ψ_k)(x) := ∫ g(t) ψ_k(x − t) dLⁿ(t) → g(x) as k → ∞, for Lⁿ-a.e. x ∈ ℝⁿ. Here ℝⁿ = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n), Lⁿ is Lebesgue measure (volume), and (g ∗ ψ_k)(x) is Lean's convolution g (ψ k) (ContinuousLinearMap.lsmul ℝ ℝ) volume x.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ n : ℕ, ∃ ψ : ℕ → Eucl n → ℝ, (∀ k, ContDiff ℝ ((⊤ : ℕ∞) : WithTop ℕ∞) (ψ k)) ∧ (∀ k, HasCompactSupport (ψ k)) ∧ (∀ k : ℕ, tsupport (ψ k) ⊆ closedBall 0 (1 / ((k : ℝ) + 1))) ∧ (∀ k y, 0 ≤ ψ k y) ∧ (∀ k, ∫ y, ψ k y ∂volume = 1) ∧ ∀ g : Eucl n → ℝ, LocallyIntegrable g volume → ∀ᵐ x ∂volume, Tendsto (fun k => convolution g (ψ k) (ContinuousLinearMap.lsmul ℝ ℝ) volume x) atTop (𝓝 (g x))
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Simon, Introduction to Geometric Measure Theory, Ch. 6, Theorem 2.34, printed proof p. 143: the mollifier ϕ_(σ)(x) = σ^{−n} ϕ(σ^{−1}x), with ϕ a mollifier as in §2 of Ch. 2 (printed p. 49: ϕ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝⁿ), ϕ ≥ 0, spt ϕ ⊆ B_1(0), ∫ϕ = 1). The printed proof concludes that θ_ε is constant on B_ρ(x₀) “letting σ ↓ 0”; this limiting fact is quoted in the bracket of Step 5 of the parent proof (“letting σ ↓ 0 (Lebesgue differentiation)”). Here σ = 1/(k+1). The a.e. convergence is derived from the Lebesgue differentiation theorem (Simon Ch. 1, Corollary 3.17) in its Lebesgue-point form.

Notation. ℝⁿ = Eucl n; Lⁿ = Lebesgue measure (volume); |·| is the Euclidean norm; B_s(x) = ball x s, B̄_s(x) = closedBall x s; spt = tsupport; ⨍_K f := Lⁿ(K)⁻¹ ∫_K f; (g ∗ ψ)(x) = ∫ g(t) ψ(x − t) dLⁿ(t) = convolution g ψ (ContinuousLinearMap.lsmul ℝ ℝ) volume x.

Proof.

1. (A fixed mollifier.) B_1(0) is a neighbourhood of 0, so there is a C^∞ function h : ℝⁿ → ℝ with compact support, spt h ⊆ B_1(0), 0 ≤ h ≤ 1 and h(0) = 1 (a smooth bump function).
- h is continuous with compact support, hence integrable. Put I := ∫ h dLⁿ.
- The set {h ≠ 0} is open (h is continuous) and contains 0, so it has positive Lebesgue measure. Since h ≥ 0 is integrable, I > 0.
- If |y| ≥ 1 then y ∉ B_1(0) ⊇ spt h, so h(y) = 0.

2. (The kernels.) For k ∈ ℕ let s_k := k + 1 > 0, r_k := 1/s_k and ψ_k(y) := s_kⁿ · I⁻¹ · h(s_k y).
(a) ψ_k is C^∞: it is a constant multiple of h composed with the linear map y ↦ s_k y.
(b) If |y| ≥ r_k then |s_k y| = s_k|y| ≥ 1, so h(s_k y) = 0 and ψ_k(y) = 0. Hence {ψ_k ≠ 0} ⊆ B̄_{r_k}(0). Since this ball is closed, spt ψ_k ⊆ B̄_{r_k}(0) = B̄_{1/(k+1)}(0).
(c) spt ψ_k is a closed subset of the compact ball B̄_{r_k}(0), so ψ_k has compact support.
(d) 0 ≤ ψ_k(y) ≤ s_kⁿ I⁻¹ for every y, since 0 ≤ h ≤ 1 and I > 0.
(e) ∫ ψ_k dLⁿ = s_kⁿ I⁻¹ ∫ h(s_k y) dy = s_kⁿ I⁻¹ · s_k^{−n} ∫ h dLⁿ = 1. This uses the linear change of variables ∫ f(R y) dy = |R|^{−n} ∫ f for R ≠ 0 (the dimension of ℝⁿ is n).
(f) ψ_k is continuous with compact support, hence integrable. Since Lⁿ is invariant under translations and under y ↦ −y, for every x the function t ↦ ψ_k(x − t) is integrable and ∫ ψ_k(x − t) dt = ∫ ψ_k = 1.
(a)–(e) prove the first five assertions.

3. (Lebesgue points.) Let g be locally integrable. By the Lebesgue differentiation theorem in Lebesgue-point form, for Lⁿ-a.e. x:
 (∗) ⨍_{B̄_r(x)} |g(t) − g(x)| dt → 0 as r ↓ 0.
[Derivation from Simon 1.3.17. For each rational q, apply 3.17 to the locally integrable function |g − q|: ⨍_{B_r(x)} |g − q| → |g(x) − q| for x outside an Lⁿ-null set N_q. Let x ∉ ⋃_{q∈ℚ} N_q and q ∈ ℚ. Then ⨍_{B_r(x)} |g − g(x)| ≤ ⨍_{B_r(x)} |g − q| + |q − g(x)|, so limsup_{r↓0} ⨍_{B_r(x)} |g − g(x)| ≤ 2|g(x) − q|, which can be made arbitrarily small. Open and closed balls differ by a null sphere. Mathlib states (∗) directly as IsUnifLocDoublingMeasure.ae_tendsto_average_norm_sub, since Lebesgue measure on ℝⁿ is uniformly locally doubling.]
Fix x satisfying (∗). Since r_k > 0 and r_k → 0, A_k := ⨍_{B̄_{r_k}(x)} |g(t) − g(x)| dt → 0 as k → ∞.

4. (The basic estimate.) Fix k and put K := B̄_{r_k}(x), a compact set.
(a) t ↦ g(t) ψ_k(x − t) is integrable. It vanishes off K, because ψ_k(x − t) = 0 when |x − t| ≥ r_k (2(b)). On K it is the product of g, which is integrable on the compact set K, with the bounded continuous function t ↦ ψ_k(x − t). (Mathlib: HasCompactSupport.convolutionExists_right.)
(b) By 2(f), t ↦ g(x) ψ_k(x − t) is integrable with integral g(x).
(c) Hence (g ∗ ψ_k)(x) − g(x) = ∫ g(t) ψ_k(x − t) dt − ∫ g(x) ψ_k(x − t) dt = ∫ (g(t) − g(x)) ψ_k(x − t) dt.
(d) Since ψ_k ≥ 0: |∫ (g(t) − g(x)) ψ_k(x − t) dt| ≤ ∫ |g(t) − g(x)| ψ_k(x − t) dt.
(e) If t ∉ K then |x − t| > r_k, so ψ_k(x − t) = 0 by 2(b). Hence ∫ |g(t) − g(x)| ψ_k(x − t) dt = ∫_K |g(t) − g(x)| ψ_k(x − t) dt.
(f) t ↦ |g(t) − g(x)| is integrable on K, because g is integrable on K and constants are integrable on the finite-measure set K. By 2(d), 0 ≤ |g(t) − g(x)| ψ_k(x − t) ≤ s_kⁿ I⁻¹ |g(t) − g(x)|. Hence ∫_K |g(t) − g(x)| ψ_k(x − t) dt ≤ s_kⁿ I⁻¹ ∫_K |g(t) − g(x)| dt.
(g) By the scaling of Lebesgue measure, Lⁿ(K) = r_kⁿ ω with ω := Lⁿ(B_1(0)) ∈ (0, ∞). Since s_kⁿ r_kⁿ = 1, s_kⁿ = ω/Lⁿ(K). So s_kⁿ I⁻¹ ∫_K |g(t) − g(x)| dt = I⁻¹ ω ⨍_K |g(t) − g(x)| dt = C A_k, where C := I⁻¹ ω does not depend on k or x.
Altogether, |(g ∗ ψ_k)(x) − g(x)| ≤ C A_k for every k.

5. (Conclusion.) 0 ≤ |(g ∗ ψ_k)(x) − g(x)| ≤ C A_k, and C A_k → 0 by Step 3, so (g ∗ ψ_k)(x) → g(x) as k → ∞ (squeeze). This holds for every x satisfying (∗), i.e. for Lⁿ-a.e. x. This proves the last assertion. ∎
(For n = 0 every step holds verbatim: ℝ⁰ is a point carrying the unit point mass, B_1(0) = ℝ⁰ and ω = 1.)

subproblem.title: Printed display (2): the density θ has vanishing weak coordinate derivatives on B_ρ(x₀)
subproblem.statement: Let n ∈ ℕ, U ⊆ ℝⁿ and u : (ℝⁿ → ℝ) → ℝ such that u(D_j a) = 0 for every C^∞ compactly supported a : ℝⁿ → ℝ with spt a ⊆ U and every j ∈ {1,…,n}. Here spt g is the closed support of g, the closure of {g ≠ 0} (Lean: tsupport g), and D_j a(x) := Da(x)(e_j), where e_j = EuclideanSpace.single j 1 is the j-th standard basis vector. Let x₀ ∈ ℝⁿ and ρ, ε ∈ ℝ with B̄_{ρ+ε}(x₀) ⊆ U, and put B := B_ρ(x₀). Let φ : ℝⁿ → ℝ be C^∞ with compact support and spt φ ⊆ B̄_ε(0). Let θ : ℝⁿ → ℝ be any function satisfying (1) u(φ ∗ (1_B f)) = ∫_B f θ dLⁿ for every f : ℝⁿ → ℝ integrable on B. Here (φ ∗ g)(x) = ∫ φ(t) g(x − t) dLⁿ(t), and 1_B f is f on B and 0 off B. All integrals are Bochner integrals with respect to Lebesgue measure Lⁿ (Lean's ∫, which is 0 for a non-integrable integrand); no measurability or integrability of θ is assumed. Then ∫_{ℝⁿ} θ(x) D_j a(x) dLⁿ(x) = 0 for every C^∞ compactly supported a : ℝⁿ → ℝ with spt a ⊆ B and every j ∈ {1,…,n}.

subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Simon, Introduction to Geometric Measure Theory, Ch. 6, Theorem 2.34 (Constancy Theorem), printed proof pp. 142–143, display (2): “∫ D_j a θ_ε dLⁿ = T(dω_j) = ∂T(ω_j) = 0, j = 1,…,n”. This child is Steps 1–4 of the accepted proof of the parent node root.constancy-a1.local_on_balls-a1.density_constancy-a1, specialized to C^∞ test functions. The hypothesis u(D_j a) = 0 plays the role of T(dω_j) = ∂T(ω_j) = 0, and the kernel φ plays the role of ϕ_ε. [Printed form: with ω_j = (−1)^{j−1} a_ε dx¹∧⋯∧dx^{j−1}∧dx^{j+1}∧⋯∧dxⁿ one has dω_j = (D_j a)_ε dx¹∧⋯∧dxⁿ, where a_ε = ϕ_ε ∗ a.]

Notation.
- ℝⁿ = Eucl n = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n); Lⁿ = Lebesgue measure (Lean: volume).
- spt g = tsupport g; B_s(x) = ball x s; B̄_s(x) = closedBall x s.
- e_j = EuclideanSpace.single j 1; D_j g(x) = Dg(x)(e_j) = fderiv ℝ g x e_j.
- (f ∗ g)(x) = ∫ f(t) g(x − t) dLⁿ(t) = convolution f g (ContinuousLinearMap.lsmul ℝ ℝ) volume x.
- 1_B f = B.indicator f; “C^∞” = ContDiff ℝ ((⊤ : ℕ∞) : WithTop ℕ∞).
- Integrals are Bochner integrals, equal to 0 for a non-integrable integrand.

Proof. Put B := B_ρ(x₀). Fix a C^∞ function a : ℝⁿ → ℝ with compact support and spt a ⊆ B, and fix j. Put v := e_j and d(x) := Da(x)(v) = D_j a(x).

1. (The function d.)
- a is C^∞, in particular C¹, so x ↦ Da(x) is continuous. Evaluation at the fixed vector v is continuous and linear, so d is continuous.
- Let x ∉ spt a. Then a vanishes on the open neighbourhood ℝⁿ ∖ spt a of x, so Da(x) = 0 and d(x) = 0. Hence {d ≠ 0} ⊆ spt a, and since spt a is closed, spt d ⊆ spt a ⊆ B.
- Consequently d has compact support (spt d is a closed subset of the compact set spt a), and d is integrable on ℝⁿ (continuous with compact support), in particular integrable on B.
- Also d(x) = 0 for every x ∉ B, and 1_B d = d.

2. (φ ∗ a is admissible for u.)
(a) φ is C^∞ with compact support and a is continuous, hence locally integrable. By differentiation under the integral sign, φ ∗ a is C^∞.
(b) φ and a both have compact support, so φ ∗ a has compact support.
(c) Suppose (φ ∗ a)(x) ≠ 0. Then the integrand t ↦ φ(t) a(x − t) is not identically 0, so x = s + t with φ(s) ≠ 0 and a(t) ≠ 0. That is, {φ ∗ a ≠ 0} ⊆ {φ ≠ 0} + {a ≠ 0}.
 For such s and t: s ∈ spt φ ⊆ B̄_ε(0), i.e. |s| ≤ ε; and t ∈ spt a ⊆ B, i.e. |t − x₀| < ρ. Hence |x − x₀| = |s + (t − x₀)| ≤ |s| + |t − x₀| ≤ ε + ρ.
 So {φ ∗ a ≠ 0} ⊆ B̄_{ρ+ε}(x₀). Since this ball is closed, spt(φ ∗ a) ⊆ B̄_{ρ+ε}(x₀) ⊆ U.
Thus φ ∗ a is C^∞, has compact support, and spt(φ ∗ a) ⊆ U.

3. (The derivative falls on a.) a is C¹ with compact support, and φ is locally integrable (it is continuous). So φ ∗ a is differentiable at every x, with D(φ ∗ a)(x) = ∫ φ(t) Da(x − t) dLⁿ(t), the convolution of φ with the continuous, compactly supported operator-valued function Da. Evaluation at the fixed vector v commutes with this integral, so D(φ ∗ a)(x)(v) = ∫ φ(t) Da(x − t)(v) dt = (φ ∗ d)(x). Hence, as functions, D_j(φ ∗ a) = φ ∗ d = φ ∗ (1_B d), the last equality because 1_B d = d (Step 1).

4. (Display (2).)
- Apply the hypothesis on u to the admissible function φ ∗ a of Step 2 and the index j: u(D_j(φ ∗ a)) = 0. By Step 3 this says u(φ ∗ (1_B d)) = 0.
- Hypothesis (1) with f := d (integrable on B by Step 1) gives ∫_B d θ dLⁿ = u(φ ∗ (1_B d)) = 0.
- The function x ↦ d(x) θ(x) vanishes for x ∉ B (Step 1), so its integral over B equals its integral over ℝⁿ. For the Bochner integral this needs no integrability: the integrand equals its restriction 1_B·(dθ), and B is measurable.
- Therefore ∫_{ℝⁿ} θ(x) D_j a(x) dLⁿ(x) = ∫_{ℝⁿ} d(x) θ(x) dLⁿ(x) = ∫_B d θ dLⁿ = 0.
Since a and j were arbitrary, the claim follows. ∎

Remark. The hypotheses 0 < ρ and 0 < ε, and any measurability or boundedness of θ, are not used and are not assumed.

subproblem.title: A locally integrable function with vanishing weak coordinate derivatives on a ball is a.e. constant there
subproblem.statement: Let n ∈ ℕ, let θ : ℝⁿ → ℝ be locally Lⁿ-integrable, x₀ ∈ ℝⁿ and ρ > 0. Assume ∫_{ℝⁿ} θ(x) D_j a(x) dLⁿ(x) = 0 for every C^∞ compactly supported a : ℝⁿ → ℝ with spt a ⊆ B_ρ(x₀) and every j ∈ {1,…,n}. Here D_j a(x) := Da(x)(e_j), e_j = EuclideanSpace.single j 1 is the j-th standard basis vector, and spt a is the closed support, the closure of {a ≠ 0} (Lean: tsupport a). Then there is c ∈ ℝ with θ(x) = c for Lⁿ-a.e. x ∈ B_ρ(x₀).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (θ : Eucl n → ℝ), LocallyIntegrable θ volume → ∀ (x₀ : Eucl n) (ρ : ℝ), 0 < ρ → (∀ a : Eucl n → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ ((⊤ : ℕ∞) : WithTop ℕ∞) a → HasCompactSupport a → tsupport a ⊆ ball x₀ ρ → ∀ j : Fin n, ∫ x, θ x * fderiv ℝ a x (EuclideanSpace.single j (1 : ℝ)) ∂volume = 0) → ∃ c : ℝ, ∀ᵐ x ∂volume.restrict (ball x₀ ρ), θ x = c
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Simon, Introduction to Geometric Measure Theory, Ch. 6, Theorem 2.34, printed proof p. 143: “If σ < … and x ∈ B_{ρ−σ}(x₀), then ϕ_(σ)(x − ·) is a C_c^∞(B_ρ(x₀)) function and hence a legitimate choice for a in (2), so in fact (2) says D_j((θ_ε)_(σ)) = 0 on B_{ρ−σ}(x₀), hence (θ_ε)_(σ) is constant on B_{ρ−σ}(x₀), hence (letting σ ↓ 0) θ_ε is constant c on B_ρ(x₀).” Some symbols are lost in the text extraction; this reading follows the bracket of Step 5 of the parent proof. Correspondences:
- the locally integrable θ plays the role of θ_ε, and the hypothesis is (2);
- the mollifiers ϕ_(σ), σ = 1/(k+1), and the limit σ ↓ 0 come from the sibling theorem smooth_approx_identity.
We mollify θ itself rather than 1_B θ. On B_{ρ−σ}(x₀) the two mollifications coincide, and since θ is locally integrable on all of ℝⁿ, θ ∗ ψ_k is defined everywhere.

Notation. ℝⁿ = Eucl n; Lⁿ = Lebesgue measure (volume); |·| = Euclidean norm; B_s(x) = ball x s, B̄_s(x) = closedBall x s; spt = tsupport; e_j = EuclideanSpace.single j 1; (θ ∗ ψ)(x) = ∫ θ(t) ψ(x − t) dLⁿ(t) = convolution θ ψ (ContinuousLinearMap.lsmul ℝ ℝ) volume x.

Proof.

1. (Mollifiers.) By the sibling theorem smooth_approx_identity (constancy_mdc_smooth_approx_identity_ae_tendsto) there are ψ_k : ℝⁿ → ℝ (k ∈ ℕ), each C^∞ with compact support and spt ψ_k ⊆ B̄_{r_k}(0), where r_k := 1/(k+1). Since θ is locally integrable, θ_k(x) := (θ ∗ ψ_k)(x) = ∫ θ(t) ψ_k(x − t) dt → θ(x) for Lⁿ-a.e. x. (The other two properties, ψ_k ≥ 0 and ∫ψ_k = 1, are not needed.)

2. (Smoothness and derivative of θ_k.) ψ_k is C^∞, in particular C¹, with compact support, and θ is locally integrable. Hence θ_k is C^∞, in particular differentiable everywhere. Differentiating under the integral sign gives Dθ_k(x) = ∫ θ(t) Dψ_k(x − t) dt. Evaluation at a fixed v commutes with this integral, since Dψ_k is continuous with compact support. So for every x and v ∈ ℝⁿ: Dθ_k(x)(v) = ∫ θ(t) Dψ_k(x − t)(v) dt.

3. (The derivative vanishes where the reflected kernel fits in the ball.) Fix k and x with B̄_{r_k}(x) ⊆ B_ρ(x₀), and let a(t) := ψ_k(x − t).
